stockRace.noLock.title: Without FOR UPDATE
stockRace.noLock.introduction: Three units of SKU-C sit in one bin. Orders A and B each want all three and arrive at the same moment. In this version the bin row is read without a lock.
stockRace.noLock.step1: A opens a transaction and reads the bin. Nothing is reserved, so all three units look available.
stockRace.noLock.step2: B does the same a moment later. A has written nothing yet, so B sees exactly what A saw: three units available.
stockRace.noLock.step3: A reserves its three units. The new value, 0 + 3, was computed in the application from what A read. Postgres takes the row lock for this write and keeps it until A commits.
stockRace.noLock.step4: B writes its own 0 + 3. Postgres makes B wait for A's row lock, so the two writes cannot interleave — but the number B is about to write was decided on a read that is already out of date.
stockRace.noLock.step5: A commits and releases the lock. B's write goes through at once and replaces A's 3 with B's 3. A's reservation has disappeared from the count, and nobody was told.
stockRace.noLock.step6: B commits. Both orders were told they hold three units: six units promised, three on the shelf.
stockRace.noLock.outcome: A lost update. The row says three are reserved, each order believes it holds three, and three units are oversold. There was no error and no constraint violation: every write stored a legal value.
stockRace.withLock.title: With FOR UPDATE
stockRace.withLock.introduction: The same shelf and the same two orders. This time the bins are read with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, which is what warehouse does.
stockRace.withLock.step1: A opens a transaction and reads the bin with FOR UPDATE. The row lock is taken at the read, so nothing can change the row between A's decision and A's write.
stockRace.withLock.step2: B asks for the same row FOR UPDATE and waits. It has not read anything yet, so it has nothing stale to act on. Warehouse bounds this wait with a lock_timeout that applies to this transaction only.
stockRace.withLock.step3: A reserves its three units, computed from the value it read under the lock.
stockRace.withLock.step4: A commits and the lock passes to B. B's read completes now and returns the row as A left it: three reserved, none available.
stockRace.withLock.step5: No bin can cover three units, so warehouse refuses with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK and rolls B's transaction back, taking B's ledger rows with it.
stockRace.withLock.outcome: Three units on the shelf, three promised. B was refused on the true count instead of being given stock that no longer existed.

saga.label.empty: No rows yet: nothing has been attempted.
saga.succeeds.title: Everything answers
saga.succeeds.introduction: A cart of two products from one merchant, with a voucher and one item on a flash sale. Before any of this, order priced the cart with pricing, wrote the order as PENDING_PAYMENT and opened a saga. Every step below is written to the saga log as Attempting before its call goes out.
saga.succeeds.step1: Redeem the voucher. pricing records a redemption row for this order — the ledger entry that makes it possible to give the voucher back later.
saga.succeeds.step2: Claim the flash-sale unit before touching the shelf. It is the scarcer resource; failing on it after reserving stock would mean undoing more.
saga.succeeds.step3: Reserve the first product in warehouse, under the row lock from the first lesson.
saga.succeeds.step4: One row per product: the second reservation is its own step, so each can be released on its own.
saga.succeeds.step5: Hold the money in escrow. payment moves it from the customer's wallet into a hold, keyed by the order number so a repeat cannot take it twice.
saga.succeeds.step6: Only now is warehouse told there is an order to pick. A fulfilment task created earlier could be picked for an order that is about to be unwound.
saga.succeeds.step7: Every hold is real, so the saga is Completed, the order becomes PAID — and only then is the cart emptied.
saga.succeeds.outcome: Six calls, six rows Done, one answer to the customer: 201 Created.
saga.refused.title: Warehouse refuses
saga.refused.introduction: The same checkout, but the shelf holds only one unit of SKU-B and the cart wants two.
saga.refused.step4: warehouse refuses SKU-B with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK, inside the same transaction that would have taken the units. Nothing is held for this row, so it is recorded Failed and will not be compensated.
saga.refused.step5: Compensation starts from the newest row and works backwards. SKU-A goes back to the shelf first.
saga.refused.step6: Then the flash-sale unit goes back to the sale.
saga.refused.step7: Then the voucher redemption is released, so the customer can use the voucher again.
saga.refused.step8: Everything is given back: the saga is Compensated and the order is kept as CANCELLED, not deleted. The customer gets 409 CHECKOUT_ROLLED_BACK with the order number and warehouse's reason.
saga.refused.outcome: Nothing is held anywhere, and the order explains itself: a cancelled checkout with a reason, not one that silently never happened.
saga.silent.title: Payment does not answer
saga.silent.introduction: The voucher and the stock are held, then the call to payment runs out of time. order cannot tell whether the hold was created before the connection gave up.
saga.silent.step3: CreateEscrowHold is written as Attempting, sent, and never answered. The row stays Attempting: order does not know whether money moved. The checkout gives up — "a service this checkout depends on did not answer" — and starts compensating.
saga.silent.step4: An Attempting row is compensated exactly like a Done one: undoing too much is safe, undoing too little strands money. The refund goes out under the same order-keyed idempotency key, and had its answer been unclear, order would read payment's ledger with GetEscrowStatus before deciding.
saga.silent.step5: SKU-A goes back to the shelf.
saga.silent.step7: The saga is Compensated and the customer gets 409 CHECKOUT_ROLLED_BACK. Whether or not the first hold had landed, nothing is held now.
saga.silent.outcome: A call with no answer is treated as possibly done. pricing and warehouse answer a release for something never taken as a success; for money, order goes further and confirms against payment's ledger before closing the row.
saga.stuck.title: A release fails
saga.stuck.introduction: warehouse refuses SKU-B again, but this time pricing is down while the saga unwinds.
saga.stuck.step3: warehouse refuses SKU-B: Failed, nothing held.
saga.stuck.step5: Releasing the voucher fails with UNAVAILABLE. A transient error neither stops the round nor counts as success: the voucher row stays Done, still held. The saga ends Stuck with its next round due in 15–30 s — and the customer already has their 409.
saga.stuck.step6: StuckSagaSweeper runs every minute and takes over due sagas under a fresh lease. The retry re-sends only what is still held: the voucher, not SKU-A.
saga.stuck.step7: The voucher comes back and the saga is Compensated. Had pricing stayed down, the delay would keep doubling up to 30 minutes, and after the sixth round the saga is Abandoned and logged GIVING UP for a person to settle.
saga.stuck.outcome: A partial unwind is never reported as a complete one. Stuck means still holding something and retrying; Abandoned means a person must look.
trust.verdict.asserted: states a fact it does not own
trust.price.title: The unit price
trust.price.introduction: Adding a product to the cart and checking out — as it worked until order v0.1.11, and as it works now.
trust.price.step1: Before: the request to add a product carried its own UnitPrice, and its title, category and merchant too. The cart stored every field exactly as sent.
trust.price.step2: At checkout, order built the price lines from the cart's numbers. pricing applied flash sales and discounts correctly — to the base price it was handed, which the buyer had written.
trust.price.step3: The escrow hold debited that figure, and the merchant would have been paid it. Any signed-in buyer could set the price of anything, and nothing failed: every service did its own job correctly.
trust.price.step4: After: the request carries only what the buyer actually decides — which product, and how many.
trust.price.step5: order asks catalog, the owner of products, for the price, title and merchant, and refreshes a line already in the cart instead of keeping the figure it was added with.
trust.price.step6: Checkout asks catalog again and prices from its answer, not from the cart. That second lookup protected carts saved before the fix, which live in Redis for fourteen days.
trust.price.outcome: The price is the one catalog holds. Fixed in order v0.1.11, and in production since 24 September 2026.
trust.shipping.title: The shipping fee
trust.shipping.introduction: Checking out with a shipping tier — as checkout worked before September 2026, and as it works now.
trust.shipping.step1: Before: the checkout request carried BaseShippingFee and DistanceKm, both defaulting to 0. A buyer who sent nothing had still sent a fee.
trust.shipping.step2: order passed the buyer's fee to pricing as the base shipping fee. pricing applied its shipping discounts on top of whatever arrived; it had no way to know the base was forged.
trust.shipping.step3: The escrow hold took the result: free shipping for anyone who asked for it.
trust.shipping.step4: After: the request names a tier — a choice — and no amount. A fee posted anyway is ignored.
trust.shipping.step5: order asks matching which courier tiers can serve the delivery, and pricing what each tier costs from its rate card. A tier that is not offered is refused rather than priced.
trust.shipping.step6: pricing's final shipping fee must be a discount of its own quote. If it is negative or above the quote, the checkout is refused before an order row exists.
trust.shipping.outcome: The fee comes from the services that own couriers and rates. A request can choose a tier; it cannot name a price.
trust.topUp.title: The wallet top-up
trust.topUp.introduction: Topping up a wallet — as it worked until 14 September 2026, and as it works now.
trust.topUp.step1: Before: a top-up request carried an amount of at least IDR 1,000, with no upper limit. The payment method was accepted and never used.
trust.topUp.step2: payment credited the wallet with that amount straight away. No charge was made, so nothing was paid.
trust.topUp.step3: The balance could then be spent through checkout escrow. Money was created by asking for it.
trust.topUp.step4: After: the amount is still the customer's choice, but only as the amount to be charged. payment records the top-up as PENDING under its Idempotency-Key, asks Midtrans to charge it, and answers 202 with payment instructions.
trust.topUp.step5: When Midtrans reports the payment, payment first verifies the notification's SHA-512 signature, then sets its contents aside and asks Midtrans's status API itself what happened to this order.
trust.topUp.step6: Only a settled payment whose amount equals the recorded one is credited — once, under a lock on the wallet's owner. Anything else credits nothing.
trust.topUp.outcome: The customer chooses how much to pay, the payment provider says what was paid, and only then does money appear. Fixed on 14 September 2026, before production launched.
idem.status.lost: done, but the answer was lost
idem.label.noRecords: Nothing is recorded: without a key there is nothing to look up.
idem.noKey.title: No key
idem.noKey.introduction: A checkout whose answer is lost on the way back — the request worked, the network did not. The client cannot tell which, so it tries again.
idem.noKey.step1: The checkout runs: an order is written and money is held in escrow.
idem.noKey.step2: The response never arrives. From the client's side, a timeout looks exactly like a checkout that never happened.
idem.noKey.step3: The client retries. Without a key the server cannot tell a retry from a second purchase, so it makes a second order and holds the money again.
idem.noKey.outcome: Two orders, two holds, one intended purchase. A server can only deduplicate what the client lets it recognise.
idem.withKey.title: With a key
idem.withKey.introduction: The same lost answer, but this time the client sent an Idempotency-Key — a value it chose once for this purchase and repeats on every retry.
idem.withKey.step1: order stores the key on the order row. A unique index on the customer and the key means there can only ever be one order under it.
idem.withKey.step3: The retry carries the same key. order finds the order already made under it and answers with that one — even while its saga is still running. Nothing new is created or charged.
idem.withKey.outcome: One order, one hold. If two copies race past the lookup at the same instant, the unique index lets one insert and makes the other fail: an error, never a second order.
idem.conflict.title: Same key, different request
idem.conflict.introduction: Between services the key is not chosen by a person: order derives it from the order number, so every retry of the same step carries the same key automatically.
idem.conflict.step1: order asks payment to hold 150.000 under the key order:ORD-1. payment records the key together with a fingerprint of the request, and applies the hold.
idem.conflict.step2: A retry arrives with the same key and the same request. payment finds the record, sees the same fingerprint and replays the stored answer. There is no second hold.
idem.conflict.step3: A request arrives with the same key but a different total. The fingerprint does not match, so payment refuses with IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED, applies nothing, and logs both fingerprints for a person to read.
idem.conflict.outcome: A key names one request, not one order. Reusing it for a different request is a bug in the caller, so it is refused rather than quietly answered with the first result.
idem.together.title: Two at once
idem.together.introduction: Two identical ReserveStock calls reach warehouse at the same moment — a retry that overtook the call it was retrying.
idem.together.step1: The first call claims the key by inserting its record, inside the transaction that will reserve the units. Until it commits, no other transaction can see that record.
idem.together.step2: The second call tries to insert the same key and blocks on the unique index — it waits for the first to finish instead of racing it.
idem.together.step3: The first commits. The second's insert now fails as a duplicate, so it reads the record and returns the first answer's exact bytes. The stock moved once.
idem.together.outcome: The database's unique index is the referee. A duplicate either waits and replays, or — if the wait outlasts the lock timeout — is told RESERVATION_IN_PROGRESS and changes nothing.
contracts.actor.author: author
contracts.additive.title: Additive
contracts.additive.introduction: A request gains a new field. Nothing that reads the message today is affected, so the change should pass every gate and reach every language.
contracts.additive.step1: The author runs buf lint. It applies buf's STANDARD rules for naming and layout, and loads moneylint — Kinetix's own buf plugin — for the two money rules. A bool called include_stock is not money, so both pass.
contracts.additive.step2: On the pull request, CI runs the breaking gate against main. buf breaking compares the new contract with main's under the FILE rules, and a new field number breaks no existing reader, so it reports nothing.
contracts.additive.step3: Pushing a release tag starts the release workflow. It runs the checks again against the previous tag, generates the code once, and publishes those same bytes to four registries. A service that does not use a package fetches the .proto files at a pinned tag and commit and generates them in its own build.
contracts.additive.outcome: A new field number costs nothing: old readers skip a field they do not know, new readers get it. No entry in the register, no coordinated deploy.
contracts.money.title: Float money
contracts.money.introduction: A shipping fee is added as a double — the type most languages reach for first when a number has decimals.
contracts.money.step1: The author adds double shipping_fee to the request. As protobuf it is perfectly valid: double is a real type and the name is well formed.
contracts.money.step2: moneylint walks every field of every message. A double or float whose name contains a money word — fee, price, total, amount and a few more — is rejected with the reason in the message, and buf lint fails.
contracts.money.step3: The breaking gate, which runs beside lint on a pull request, passes: adding a field breaks no reader. Compatible and correct are different questions. Even a tag cut from this commit would publish nothing, because the release workflow runs buf lint again before it generates any code.
contracts.money.outcome: Money in Kinetix is common.v1.Money — an integer count of minor units and a currency code. The rule lives in the contract, so no service has to remember it: a float amount never reaches a single generated file.
contracts.accidental.title: Accidental break
contracts.accidental.introduction: A field that looks unused is deleted from a response.
contracts.accidental.step1: The author deletes bool found = 1 from GetProductResponse. It still lints: a message without that field is well formed.
contracts.accidental.step2: buf breaking reports the deleted field. The gate looks in docs/BREAKING.md for an unreleased version that declares it, finds none, and fails with the finding and what to do about it.
contracts.accidental.outcome: Merged, every service built against the old contract would read found as false — the proto3 default — on every product: not an error, a wrong answer. The gate turns that into a red check before anything is generated.
contracts.declared.title: Declared break
contracts.declared.introduction: Sometimes the break is the fix. Two identity responses carried bool has_location beside a GeoPoint location. In C++, protoc generates has_location() for the message field's presence and has_location() for the boolean — two members with one name, which no compiler accepts. The communication service, written in C++, could not compile the contract at all.
contracts.declared.step1: The flag is deleted from both messages, and field numbers 10 and 8 are reserved, so neither can return meaning something else.
contracts.declared.step2: The author declares the break in docs/BREAKING.md under v1.0.20: buf's findings word for word, the reason, what each language changes, and which service to deploy first.
contracts.declared.step3: At the tag, the release workflow runs the gate against v1.0.19. Each finding matches a declared line exactly, so the gate passes, and v1.0.20 is generated and published.
contracts.declared.outcome: The gate has no skip flag. The only way past it is to write the break down in the file a consumer reads before bumping a pin — and a declared line that matches no real finding excuses nothing.
outage.price.title: Price
outage.price.introduction: Checkout asks pricing for the total. A flash sale is running: the item lists at 200.000 and sells at 150.000, and shipping is 15.000.
outage.price.step1: pricing answers. The flash sale applies, shipping is added, and the order is placed at 165.000.
outage.price.step2: pricing does not answer. The old client caught every exception and priced the cart by itself — list price, no flash sale, no discount, no voucher. Checkout succeeded at 215.000, and only a log line said anything was wrong.
outage.price.step3: The client now throws PricingUnavailableException and checkout answers 503. No order is written, nothing is charged or reserved, and the customer is told to try again.
outage.price.outcome: A price nobody quoted is not a price. When the service that owns the number cannot be asked, checkout stops.
outage.stock.title: Stock
outage.stock.introduction: The product list asks warehouse how many of each item are left.
outage.stock.step1: warehouse answers: none left. The listing says out of stock, and that is true.
outage.stock.step2: warehouse does not answer. The old client returned the same record it used for a SKU warehouse had never heard of — zero available — so the listing said out of stock to a customer who could have bought.
outage.stock.step3: The client now returns a record with no quantity at all. The listing says available_stock null and stock_status unknown, which a storefront can show as "availability unknown" instead of "sold out".
outage.stock.outcome: A read may degrade instead of failing — but only into an answer that admits it does not know. Unknown is a third state, not a zero.
outage.merchant.title: Merchant
outage.merchant.introduction: A merchant creates a product. catalog first asks identity whether this merchant may sell.
outage.merchant.step1: identity answers: the merchant is suspended. catalog refuses with 403 and identity's reason — a real refusal from the service that owns the fact.
outage.merchant.step2: identity does not answer. The old client returned None, the same value as "no such merchant", and a verified merchant was told their account is not verified — a problem with their account that does not exist.
outage.merchant.step3: The client now raises IdentityUnavailableError, and catalog answers 503 with Retry-After. Nothing was created, and the account was not judged.
outage.merchant.outcome: Authorisation has three outcomes: allowed, refused, and could not check. Only the service that owns the fact may say refused.
outage.token.title: Token
outage.token.introduction: Every signed-in request carries a token signed by identity. catalog verifies it against identity's published signing keys, the JWKS.
outage.token.step1: The key set answers, and no key in it matches the one the token names. identity did not sign this token: 401 is the truth.
outage.token.step2: The key set cannot be fetched. The old code caught every exception the same way and answered 401 Invalid token. A client that trusts a 401 throws away a valid session, so a short outage of one endpoint can sign real users out.
outage.token.step3: Only a key-id mismatch is still a verdict on the token. A connection failure, an empty key set or HTML where JSON should be is now 503, and the body says the token was not rejected.
outage.token.outcome: 401 is a statement about the token. When the keys could not be read, nothing was learned about the token — so 401 is the one thing not to say.
mesh.none.title: No certificate
mesh.none.introduction: A process that can reach pricing's port opens a connection, but holds no certificate. On a network that only asks for TLS, it could now send requests.
mesh.none.step1: The process starts a TLS handshake. pricing answers with its own certificate and, because its TLS configuration names a client CA, asks the caller for one in return.
mesh.none.step2: The caller has none, so the handshake ends with the alert certificate required. No connection exists, so no request exists either, and the allow list is never consulted. The caller sees only UNAVAILABLE.
mesh.none.outcome: Naming a client CA on the server is what turns TLS into mutual TLS. Without it, the server proves who it is and the caller stays anonymous.
mesh.impostor.title: Forged identity
mesh.impostor.introduction: Anyone can write spiffe://kinetix.local/service/order into a certificate. This one was made for this run with a throwaway CA, and names order exactly.
mesh.impostor.step1: The impostor presents the certificate. Its SPIFFE ID is, letter for letter, the one order's real certificate carries.
mesh.impostor.step2: The signature chain is checked against Kinetix's CA and nothing else. The forged certificate does not chain to it, so the handshake ends with the alert unknown CA — before anything reads the name inside.
mesh.impostor.outcome: An identity is only as good as the signature on it. Who signed the certificate is checked first, and only against Kinetix's own CA, never the public roots a browser trusts.
mesh.payment.title: Valid, not allowed
mesh.payment.introduction: payment holds a real certificate from Kinetix's CA. It just has no business calling pricing.
mesh.payment.step1: payment presents its certificate, which names spiffe://kinetix.local/service/payment.
mesh.payment.step2: The chain is valid, so the TLS handshake succeeds. mTLS has now proved that the caller is a Kinetix service — which every Kinetix service can prove.
mesh.payment.step3: PeerGuard reads the SPIFFE ID from the certificate's URI SAN, takes the service name after /service/, and looks for it on the allow list. payment is not there: PERMISSION_DENIED. The caller is told only that it is not permitted; the log names who was refused.
mesh.payment.outcome: mTLS answers "is this one of ours?". Only the allow list answers "is this a caller pricing expects?".
mesh.order.title: Allowed
mesh.order.introduction: order calls pricing during every checkout, and is the one caller on this run's allow list.
mesh.order.step1: order presents its certificate, which names spiffe://kinetix.local/service/order.
mesh.order.step2: The chain is valid, and the handshake succeeds exactly as it did for payment.
mesh.order.step3: The SPIFFE ID names order, order is on the list, and the call goes through: the run asked pricing for its service list and got it. The log records which service called.
mesh.order.outcome: Every accepted call carries a cryptographic answer to "who is calling?", and the log keeps it.
refresh.ordinary.title: Ordinary
refresh.ordinary.introduction: A signed-in customer's app holds a refresh token, R1. Each time its fifteen-minute access token expires, the app trades the refresh token for a new pair.
refresh.ordinary.step1: The app presents R1. identity marks R1 used, records that R2 replaced it, and returns a new access token with R2. Every token R1 leads to belongs to one family.
refresh.ordinary.step2: Fifteen minutes later the app presents R2 and gets R3. A refresh token works exactly once.
refresh.ordinary.outcome: Rotation keeps each refresh token single-use, and the family records the chain. That record is what lets the next tabs catch a stolen copy.
refresh.replayed.title: Replayed
refresh.replayed.introduction: A copy of R1 has leaked — from a log, a backup, a compromised device. The owner keeps using the app.
refresh.replayed.step1: The owner refreshes R1 as usual and moves on to R2. The copy the thief holds is now spent.
refresh.replayed.step2: The thief presents R1. It has already been used, which can only mean two parties hold it. identity cannot tell which one is honest, so it revokes the whole family.
refresh.replayed.step3: The owner's next refresh with R2 is refused too. The session is over for both, and the owner signs in again with a password.
refresh.replayed.outcome: Reuse detection turns a silent theft into a visible event. The honest user is signed out as well — the price of not being able to tell the two apart.
refresh.thiefFirst.title: Thief first
refresh.thiefFirst.introduction: This time the thief uses the stolen R1 before the owner does.
refresh.thiefFirst.step1: The thief refreshes R1 and receives R2. For now the thief holds a working session.
refresh.thiefFirst.step2: When the owner's app presents R1, it has already been used. identity revokes the family — including the R2 the thief is holding.
refresh.thiefFirst.step3: The thief's next refresh fails. Whoever goes first, the stolen line ends the next time the owner refreshes.
refresh.thiefFirst.outcome: The thief keeps the session only until the owner's app next refreshes, plus whatever is left of the last access token it was given.
refresh.together.title: Same instant
refresh.together.introduction: Owner and thief present R1 within the same few milliseconds. Run against identity's own token service and a real Postgres, this case behaved differently before and after a fix.
refresh.together.step1: Both requests carry R1 and reach identity at once.
refresh.together.step2: Before the fix, each request read R1, saw it unused, and minted a new pair before either marked it used. Both got through — in 20 of 20 races in the run — leaving two live branches and nothing revoked.
refresh.together.step3: After the fix, rotation runs in a transaction that locks R1's row first. The first request holds the lock; the second waits for it.
refresh.together.step4: The first commits R2 and marks R1 used. Only then does the second read R1, find it used, and revoke the family — including the R2 just issued.
refresh.together.step5: So whichever request won, its new token is already dead: neither copy keeps the session.
refresh.together.outcome: A check followed by a write is a race. Lock the row, or make the write conditional, so the second caller sees what the first did.
